title: A Path Is Not a Pump

scenes.tts: If a membrane protein opens a path, can it make a solute travel uphill? The answer separates a doorway from a pump. Follow one charged solute across this membrane.
scenes.visual: Fill at least 60% of the frame height with one horizontal schematic bilayer: blue water above and below, a broad gold oily core, and no molecular structures. A yellow charged-solute circle drifts in looping Brownian motion above the bilayer. During the first question, a teal doorway outline opens through the core and the solute approaches it; a large uphill arrow rises beyond the doorway but remains dim. On 'doorway' the pore brightens; on 'pump' the pore compresses into an alternating-access gate with a small energy badge. Keep water motes and the solute moving throughout. No title is visible yet.
scenes.narration: If a membrane protein opens a path, can it make a solute travel uphill? The answer separates a doorway from a pump. Follow one charged solute across this membrane.

scenes.visual: Over the same moving water-and-membrane world, briefly place the centered title 'A Path Is Not a Pump' in large high-contrast type. The yellow solute continues drifting behind it and the bilayer gently ripples. Fade the title away by two seconds, leaving the membrane in the same position for the next scene.

scenes.tts: In water, a charged solute wears a water shell. To enter the oily bilayer core, it must lose that help. The core offers almost nothing in return. This energy cost is the toll for leaving water.
scenes.visual: Keep the carried membrane. Surround the yellow solute with six small blue water droplets labelled together 'water shell'; rotate them slowly as the solute approaches the gold core. On 'must lose', peel the droplets away one by one while a vertical energy bar marked 'schematic' beside the membrane rises red. The bare solute recoils into the upper water. On 'toll for leaving water', label the red bar with those words and let it pulse while water motes keep circulating.
scenes.narration: In water, a charged solute wears a water shell. To enter the oily bilayer core, it must lose that help. The core offers almost nothing in return. This energy cost is the toll for leaving water.

scenes.tts: A channel offers a polar pathway through the oil. Its polar groups replace some help from water, lowering the toll. Solute now crosses much faster. Yet the open channel supplies no directional energy.
scenes.visual: Transform the red toll bar into a teal pore spanning the same bilayer. Draw the pore as two simple curved walls with four moving blue grip dots, labelled 'polar pathway' and explicitly 'schematic'. As the yellow solute enters, its water droplets hand off to the grip dots, then reform below. Animate three solutes streaming downward at staggered times. On 'no directional energy', remove any motor badge and keep only a two-headed faint arrow through the open pore.
scenes.narration: A channel offers a polar pathway through the oil. Its polar groups replace some help from water, lowering the toll. Solute now crosses much faster. Yet the open channel supplies no directional energy.

scenes.tts: Direction comes from the solute's electrochemical gradient. Concentration pushes from the crowded side. Voltage pulls opposite charges and pushes like charges. Together, those pushes define downhill.
scenes.visual: Keep the membrane and channel at center. Multiply yellow solutes above and leave only two below, all drifting; give every solute a small plus sign. A blue 'concentration' arrow grows downward from the crowded side. Then place minus signs along the lower water and plus signs along the upper edge; a red 'voltage' arrow for the positive solute also grows downward. Merge both arrows into one thick green arrow labelled 'electrochemical downhill'. Solutes continue moving down the channel while both fields gently pulse.
scenes.narration: Direction comes from the solute's electrochemical gradient. Concentration pushes from the crowded side. Voltage pulls opposite charges and pushes like charges. Together, those pushes define downhill.

scenes.tts: Here, sodium is more concentrated outside, while the cell interior is negative. If a sodium channel opens, which way will sodium move? Follow both pushes before you answer.
scenes.caption: Here, Na⁺ is more concentrated outside, while the cell interior is negative. If a Na⁺ channel opens, which way will Na⁺ move? Follow both pushes before you answer.
scenes.visual: Relabel the upper side 'outside: high sodium' and the lower side 'inside: negative', using yellow sodium circles with plus signs. Close the teal channel at first. As the question is asked, open it and replace the merged arrow with two incomplete arrow outlines, one tagged 'concentration' and one 'voltage'. A large question mark appears between them. Sodium circles drift on both sides but none crosses yet.
scenes.narration: Here, Na⁺ is more concentrated outside, while the cell interior is negative. If a Na⁺ channel opens, which way will Na⁺ move? Follow both pushes before you answer.

scenes.visual: Hold the exact prediction layout and the full question 'Which way will sodium move?' in large type above the membrane. Slowly brighten each unfinished arrow in turn without revealing its direction. Sodium circles continue Brownian motion, minus signs softly pulse inside, and a thin four-and-a-half-second thinking ring closes around the question mark. No sodium crosses during the pause.

scenes.tts: Concentration pushes sodium inward, away from the crowded outside. The negative interior also pulls positive sodium inward. Both pushes agree, so opening the channel speeds sodium downhill into the cell.
scenes.caption: Concentration pushes Na⁺ inward, away from the crowded outside. The negative interior also pulls positive Na⁺ inward. Both pushes agree, so opening the channel speeds Na⁺ downhill into the cell.
scenes.visual: Resolve the two incomplete outlines into parallel downward arrows, blue for concentration and red for voltage. Merge them into the thick green 'downhill' arrow used earlier. Send sodium circles through the open channel one after another, with their speed visibly increasing after the merge. Keep the outside crowd dispersing and the inside minus signs pulsing. The question mark shrinks into a green check without changing the layout.
scenes.narration: Concentration pushes Na⁺ inward, away from the crowded outside. The negative interior also pulls positive Na⁺ inward. Both pushes agree, so opening the channel speeds Na⁺ downhill into the cell.

scenes.tts: Now reverse the combined electrochemical gradient. The same open channel lets sodium run the opposite way. The protein changes speed, not the downhill direction. A protein can change speed, but uphill transport requires energy coupling.
scenes.caption: Now reverse the combined electrochemical gradient. The same open channel lets Na⁺ run the opposite way. The protein changes speed, not the downhill direction. A protein can change speed, but uphill transport requires energy coupling.
scenes.visual: Without cutting away, slide the crowd of sodium circles to the inside and reverse the voltage signs, relabelling the sides 'outside: low sodium' and 'inside: positive', so the thick computed-from-the-two-arrows downhill arrow rotates upward. Sodium reverses through the same open teal channel. On 'changes speed', a small speed gauge marked 'schematic' rises while the arrow direction stays fixed. On the guiding sentence, freeze neither object: the gauge oscillates and solutes keep streaming while a crossed-out 'uphill' arrow points inward (downward), against the reversed gradient, never upward.
scenes.narration: Now reverse the combined electrochemical gradient. The same open channel lets Na⁺ run the opposite way. The protein changes speed, not the downhill direction. A protein can change speed, but uphill transport requires energy coupling.

scenes.tts: Channels are pores, open to both sides when their gates open. Carriers instead bind cargo, change shape, and release it across the membrane. Either mechanism can move a solute downhill without supplying energy.
scenes.visual: Split the same membrane into two adjacent working regions. On the left, keep the open teal channel with yellow solutes streaming through. On the right, transform a copy into a large schematic carrier cup: it opens upward, catches one yellow cargo circle, closes, rocks in place within the bilayer (it never travels across), opens downward, and releases it. Label only 'channel: pore' and 'carrier: alternating access'. A shared green downhill arrow sweeps behind both mechanisms.
scenes.narration: Channels are pores, open to both sides when their gates open. Carriers instead bind cargo, change shape, and release it across the membrane. Either mechanism can move a solute downhill without supplying energy.

scenes.tts: A pump is a carrier coupled directly to an energy source. This view shows only sodium from the sodium-potassium pump. A T P drives its shape change and sodium uphill, charging the gradient battery.
scenes.caption: A pump is a carrier coupled directly to an energy source. This view shows only Na⁺ from the Na⁺-K⁺ pump. ATP drives its shape change and Na⁺ uphill, charging the gradient battery.
scenes.visual: Enlarge the right-hand carrier until it dominates the carried membrane; keep it schematic and label it 'sodium-potassium pump' with a smaller 'sodium side only' tag. A green ATP block docks, transforms into a dim ADP block that drifts away while its phosphate dot stays attached to the carrier; the carrier rocks, and the phosphate leaves only later in the cycle. Move a labelled sodium circle upward against a downward green gradient arrow; reset and repeat without implying a stoichiometric count. Show the outside crowd growing. A battery outline beside the crowd fills from empty to full as repeated carrier cycles continue.
scenes.narration: A pump is a carrier coupled directly to an energy source. This view shows only Na⁺ from the Na⁺-K⁺ pump. ATP drives its shape change and Na⁺ uphill, charging the gradient battery.

scenes.tts: In one animal-cell example, a coupled carrier spends that stored gradient. Sodium runs downhill through the carrier. Glucose travels uphill in the same direction. No A T P is spent there, but the sodium gradient ultimately depends on the pump.
scenes.caption: In one animal-cell example, a coupled carrier spends that stored gradient. Na⁺ runs downhill through the carrier. Glucose travels uphill in the same direction. No ATP is spent there, but the Na⁺ gradient ultimately depends on the pump.
scenes.visual: Keep the filled sodium battery and the crowded outside. Slide the pump left but leave it cycling slowly. Transform the right region into one large schematic coupled carrier labelled 'sodium-glucose carrier'. Two yellow sodium circles roll down a green gradient ramp into the carrier with each glucose; their motion turns a visible gear that lifts a blue glucose block up its own red ramp into the cell. Show no ATP block at this carrier. Connect a thin animated line back to the sodium battery and pump on 'ultimately depends'.
scenes.narration: In one animal-cell example, a coupled carrier spends that stored gradient. Na⁺ runs downhill through the carrier. Glucose travels uphill in the same direction. No ATP is spent there, but the Na⁺ gradient ultimately depends on the pump.

scenes.tts: Classify any crossing with three questions. Is the route a pore or alternating access? Is the solute moving downhill or uphill? If uphill, what supplies energy: A T P or another downhill flow?
scenes.caption: Classify any crossing with three questions. Is the route a pore or alternating access? Is the solute moving downhill or uphill? If uphill, what supplies energy: ATP or another downhill flow?
scenes.visual: Pull back slightly while keeping the membrane across the frame. Above the left channel, morph its outline into the short label 'pore'; above the right carrier, morph its rocking motion into 'alternating access'. A yellow test solute travels along a green downhill arrow, then resets and faces a red uphill arrow. On the last question, an ATP block and a second green downhill solute appear as two alternative energy inputs, each briefly driving the carrier through one cycle.
scenes.narration: Classify any crossing with three questions. Is the route a pore or alternating access? Is the solute moving downhill or uphill? If uphill, what supplies energy: ATP or another downhill flow?

scenes.tts: Opening a channel or cycling a passive carrier cannot push a solute against its gradient. Look for energy coupling before calling transport uphill. Only coupled energy can drive transport uphill.
scenes.visual: Return to the opening composition: one membrane, one teal doorway, one yellow solute, and the large uphill arrow. Let the unpowered doorway open; the solute approaches but slides back downhill. Then attach first an ATP block and then a downhill partner solute to the carrier, each making the yellow solute advance uphill. On the final sentence, both energy sources glow while the uphill arrow becomes solid and the battery gauge continues a slow pulse.
scenes.narration: Opening a channel or cycling a passive carrier cannot push a solute against its gradient. Look for energy coupling before calling transport uphill. Only coupled energy can drive transport uphill.

scenes.visual: End card over the gently moving carried membrane. Center the rule 'Only coupled energy can drive transport uphill.' in large high-contrast type, no more than seven words. Keep one small yellow solute moving steadily up a green arrow powered by a softly pulsing ATP block; water motes drift until the final frame.
